Target ~5,000 words. See `research/00-book-outline.md` Chapter 4. Open with a real production architecture (Anterior AI + Reducto on prior-auth, 99.24% accuracy). The three patterns + decision tree are the load-bearing artifacts.

## The three reference architectures

### Pattern A: Single-pass VLM

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Single-pass VLM architecture"
flowchart LR
    A[Document image] --> B[VLM]
    B --> C[Structured output]
```

- When this works: well-formed PDFs, small variety, low stakes, simple schemas.
- When this fails: tables (consistently), dense layouts, long documents, anything requiring cross-region reasoning.
- Cost profile: lowest per-page. Highest cost-per-correct-extraction in high-variability workloads.
- Representative examples: hyperscaler APIs in their default mode; Qwen3-VL used naively.

### Pattern B: Agentic loop with reflection

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Agentic loop with reflection"
flowchart LR
    A[Document] --> B[Plan]
    B --> C[Extract pass]
    C --> D{Confidence ok?}
    D -- No --> E[Reflect / re-prompt]
    E --> C
    D -- Yes --> F[Validate]
    F --> G{Schema ok?}
    G -- No --> E
    G -- Yes --> H[Output + provenance]
```

- The "default" 2026 architecture for general-purpose agentic OCR.
- Plan → extract → critique → re-prompt → validate, with retry budgets and explicit confidence gates.
- Representative examples: LlamaParse Agentic / Agentic Plus, Landing AI ADE, Mistral OCR 3.
- Failure modes: silent hallucinations (the reflect step approves a wrong answer), retry-budget thrashing, unbounded latency.

### Pattern C: Hybrid CV + VLM (Reducto-style)

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Hybrid CV + VLM architecture"
flowchart LR
    A[Document] --> B[Layout detector / CV]
    B --> C[Region routing]
    C --> D1[Text blocks → OCR]
    C --> D2[Tables → table extractor]
    C --> D3[Figures → VLM]
    D1 & D2 & D3 --> E[Assembler]
    E --> F[Validator]
    F --> G[Output]
```

- Layout-first segmentation, route to specialized extractors, assemble, validate.
- State-of-the-art on adversarial tables: Reducto ~0.90 similarity on RD-TableBench, ~20pp ahead of hyperscalers.
- Representative examples: Reducto; IBM Granite-Docling + Docling ensemble pipelines; PP-StructureV3 lineage.
- Engineering cost is real: more components, more failure surface, more eval surface. Pays off on high-stakes, high-variability workloads.

## Tool chains, memory, and HITL gates

- Tool inventory in a production agentic OCR system: layout detector, table extractor, schema validator, KB lookup, redaction, classification, fallback OCR.
- Memory: short-term (page-local context) vs. long-term (cross-document priors, vendor-specific corrections from HITL).
- HITL gates: where they go in the loop (post-validation, pre-output), how they feed back into memory, how their accept/reject rate becomes the production accuracy signal (Chapter 11).

## Choosing between the three patterns

- Decision-tree diagram (refined version of the one in Chapter 9).
- The two axes that matter: **document variability** (narrow vs. wide) and **stakes** (low vs. high).
- Narrow + low: Pattern A is fine.
- Wide + low: Pattern B.
- High stakes (any variability): Pattern C with HITL.

## Named takes

> *"If your architecture has no place for a table-specific tool, you're betting the model is uniformly good at everything. Twelve months of leaderboards say it isn't."*

> *"Hybrid CV+VLM is winning the table benchmarks for the same reason ensembles win on tabular ML: specialization beats generality where the distribution is narrow and the stakes are high."*
